title: Module 1 – Qubits & Quantum States
objectives: Calculate computational-basis probabilities from normalized amplitudes. Distinguish a pure state vector from its Bloch-sphere representation. Predict the state after an ideal computational-basis measurement. Predict how X prepares |1⟩ from |0⟩.
introduction: A qubit is a quantum system with two computational-basis states, |0⟩ and |1⟩. Intuition: amplitudes are ingredients that can reinforce or cancel when gates combine them. More precisely, a pure qubit state is a normalized complex vector; amplitudes determine probabilities but are not themselves probabilities. This distinction is the starting point for interference.

sections.title: 1.1 States and amplitudes
sections.description: We describe pure states as |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, where α and β may be complex and |α|² + |β|² = 1. The basis vectors |0⟩ and |1⟩ are orthogonal. Multiplying the whole vector by a phase e^{iγ} changes no observable predictions: global phase is physically irrelevant. Relative phase between amplitudes can matter. The X gate swaps |0⟩ and |1⟩, so X prepares |1⟩ from |0⟩.

sections.title: 1.2 Superposition and the Bloch sphere
sections.description: Superposition depends on the chosen basis. The state |+⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2 is a superposition in the computational basis, but is itself one vector of the X basis. The Bloch sphere represents pure single-qubit states on its surface, after ignoring global phase. Its Cartesian coordinates are not the amplitudes α and β. Mixed single-qubit states lie inside the sphere; arbitrary multi-qubit states need a richer description.
sections.diagram:
|ψ⟩ = cos(θ/2)|0⟩ + e^{iφ} sin(θ/2)|1⟩
(up to global phase; θ, φ are Bloch-sphere angles)

sections.title: 1.3 Born probabilities and state update
sections.description: An ideal computational-basis measurement returns 0 with probability |α|² or 1 with probability |β|². Conditioned on the result, the state updates to the observed basis state. This update is often called collapse; here it specifies a measurement model, not a settled physical interpretation. Measuring an already prepared basis state leaves it unchanged.
sections.diagram:
P(0) = |α|²; P(1) = |β|²
Observed 0: post-measurement state |0⟩
Observed 1: post-measurement state |1⟩

workedExample: Prepare |ψ⟩ = (1/√3)|0⟩ + i√(2/3)|1⟩. The squared magnitudes sum to 1, so P(0)=1/3 and P(1)=2/3. The factor i is a phase, not a negative probability. If the result is 1, an immediate repeat measurement returns 1 in the ideal model unless a gate intervenes. By comparison H|0⟩ = |+⟩ gives probabilities 1/2 and 1/2. Repeated shots require fresh preparation; finite counts need not split exactly in half.
keyTakeaways:
• Amplitudes are complex; squared magnitudes give probabilities.
• Normalization makes the total probability 1.
• Global phase is unobservable; relative phase can affect interference.
• Computational-basis measurement updates the state conditionally.

questions.question: For |ψ⟩ = (1/√3)|0⟩ + i√(2/3)|1⟩, what is P(1) in the computational basis?
questions.explanation: The Born rule uses |i√(2/3)|² = 2/3; the complex phase has magnitude 1.

questions.question: Which pair of amplitudes is normalized?
questions.explanation: Each squared magnitude is 1/2, giving total probability 1.

questions.question: A computational-basis measurement returns 0. With no intervening gate, what does an immediate ideal repeat return?
questions.explanation: The conditional state is |0⟩, whose computational-basis outcome is 0 with probability 1.

Predict the state after an ideal computational-basis measurement.
Predict how X prepares |1⟩ from |0⟩.

experiments.expectedResult: Ideal probabilities 1/2 each; finite counts fluctuate.

title: Module 2 – Superposition
objectives: Expand a tensor product of two single-qubit states. Distinguish a product superposition from an entangled pure state. Explain why state-space dimension is not freely readable classical storage. Predict how a second Hadamard layer reverses a product superposition.
introduction: Combining qubits enlarges the space of possible amplitudes. A useful quantum algorithm shapes those amplitudes through interference so that a measurement reveals useful information. It does not expose every possible answer in one readout.

sections.title: 2.1 Hadamard and interference
sections.description: The Hadamard gate maps |0⟩ to |+⟩ and |1⟩ to |−⟩ = (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2. Applying H twice returns the starting state. Predict why two applications do not merely produce more randomness: contributions to one amplitude cancel.

sections.title: 2.2 Tensor products and entanglement
sections.description: The tensor product combines subsystem spaces. For a product state, multiply the individual amplitudes to obtain joint amplitudes. A general pure n-qubit state is a vector in a 2^n-dimensional Hilbert space, but need not factor into individual qubit states. For example (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 cannot factor: it is entangled, as Module 4 explores. We write IQLRS basis strings as |q(n−1)…q0⟩; q0 is the rightmost bit.

sections.title: 2.3 Dimension and accessible outcomes
sections.description: In |ψ⟩ = Σₓ αₓ|x⟩, normalization requires Σₓ |αₓ|² = 1 and P(x)=|αₓ|². Measuring all n qubits in the computational basis yields one n-bit string per preparation, not a list of 2^n amplitudes. Estimating a state requires many preparations and measurement settings. The exponential dimension is not 2^n freely readable classical bits.
sections.diagram:
3 qubits: 8 basis states
Equal amplitudes: 1/√8
P(101) = 1/8

workedExample: Starting at |q1 q0⟩ = |00⟩, apply H(q0) then H(q1). The state is |+⟩ ⊗ |+⟩ = (|00⟩ + |01⟩ + |10⟩ + |11⟩)/2. Each outcome has probability 1/4; the state is a product. Applying H to both again restores |00⟩ by interference. Compare the Bell state (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2: only 00 and 11 occur, each with probability 1/2, and the state is entangled.
keyTakeaways:
• Tensor products build joint spaces; only product states factor into individual states.
• A superposition of several basis states need not be entangled.
• 2^n amplitudes describe a pure state, not 2^n readable classical bits.
• Interference depends on amplitude signs and phases.

questions.question: Which normalized state is a product superposition of two |+⟩ states?
questions.explanation: Distributing the tensor product multiplies two factors of 1/√2, giving amplitude 1/2 for every basis state.

questions.question: In an equal superposition of all eight 3-qubit basis states, what is P(101)?
questions.explanation: The amplitude magnitude is 1/√8, so its square is 1/8. A shot returns one string.

questions.question: Starting from |0⟩, apply H twice with no measurement between them. What is the final state?
questions.explanation: H²=I. The amplitude contributions for |1⟩ cancel, while those for |0⟩ add.

title: Module 3 – Measurement
objectives: Calculate projective-measurement probabilities in a specified basis. Predict repeated measurements after a state update. Explain conditional Bell correlations without faster-than-light signalling.
introduction: Measurement connects quantum amplitudes to observed data. Its outcome depends on both preparation and measurement basis. We use ideal projective measurements; real devices can add readout errors. A single outcome generally does not reveal the original state.

sections.title: 3.1 Computational basis
sections.description: For a normalized pure state α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, the Born probabilities are |α|² and |β|². A projective measurement updates the state to the observed basis vector. It need not erase all information: a basis state survives a measurement in that basis.
sections.diagram:
P(0)=|α|²; P(1)=|β|²
Prepare |0⟩ → measure Z → 0 with probability 1

sections.title: 3.2 Changing the measurement basis
sections.description: For an orthonormal basis {|φᵢ⟩}, P(φᵢ)=|⟨φᵢ|ψ⟩|² and the conditional post-measurement state is |φᵢ⟩. The X basis is {|+⟩,|−⟩}. In IQLRS, applying H before computational-basis measurement implements X-basis outcome statistics: 0 labels + and 1 labels −. The physical wire after this rotated measurement is in |0⟩ or |1⟩; apply H afterward to represent the corresponding X eigenstate.
sections.diagram:
Prepare |+⟩
Z measurement: P(0)=P(1)=1/2
X measurement: P(+)=1; P(−)=0

sections.title: 3.3 Correlations without signalling
sections.description: For the Bell pair |Φ+⟩=(|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2, learning one computational-basis result lets us condition the joint-state description and predict the matching result on the other qubit. The local result remains random. Without Alice’s result, Bob sees the same local statistics whether Alice measured or not; her choice cannot carry a controllable faster-than-light signal. Comparing correlations requires classical communication.
sections.diagram:
Bell pair: P(00)=P(11)=1/2
Bob alone: P(0)=P(1)=1/2
Condition on Alice=0: Bob=0 in this basis

workedExample: Prepare (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 in |q1 q0⟩ order. Measure q0 into c0 and q1 into c1. The displayed classical string c1c0 is 00 or 11 with probability 1/2 each. If only q0 is measured and its result is 0, the conditional joint state is |00⟩. Bob holding q1 cannot tell from his local outcomes whether that distant measurement occurred. Repeated shots estimate probabilities; one shot is not state tomography.
keyTakeaways:
• Specify preparation and measurement basis before predicting probabilities.
• State update is conditional on a recorded result.
• An outcome does not uniquely identify an unknown preparation.
• Entangled correlations preserve no-signalling.

questions.question: Prepare |+⟩ and measure in the X basis {|+⟩,|−⟩}. What is P(+)?
questions.explanation: The overlap ⟨+|+⟩ is 1, so its squared magnitude is 1.

questions.question: Prepare |0⟩ and measure in the X basis. What are the probabilities?
options: The original state can be reconstructed from this one outcome
questions.explanation: |0⟩=(|+⟩+|−⟩)/√2; each squared overlap is 1/2.

questions.question: Can Alice signal a chosen bit by deciding whether to measure her half of |Φ+⟩, while Bob sees only his local outcomes?
options: Yes, Alice can choose her random measurement outcome
No, Bob’s unconditioned local statistics are unchanged
Only if Alice measures in the computational basis
questions.explanation: Bob’s local statistics are unchanged when Alice’s outcomes are not supplied. Correlations become visible when records are compared.

learningObjectives: Calculate projective-measurement probabilities in a specified basis.
Predict repeated measurements after a state update.
Explain conditional Bell correlations without faster-than-light signalling.

title: Module 4 – Entanglement & Bell States
objectives: Identify entanglement for pure two-qubit states. Construct |Φ+⟩ using H and CNOT. Explain which Bell-state distinctions computational-basis measurements hide.
introduction: Entanglement describes a joint state that cannot be assembled from independent pure subsystem states. Bell states make this concrete. Their same-basis correlations are useful, but seeing matching random bits alone is not a Bell-inequality test.

sections.title: 4.1 Pure-state entanglement
sections.description: A pure two-qubit state is entangled if it cannot be written as |a⟩ ⊗ |b⟩. For (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2, a product would need nonzero amplitudes for both 00 and 11, forcing nonzero cross terms 01 and 10, which are absent. This definition is scoped to pure states; mixed-state separability needs a more general definition.
sections.diagram:
Product: |+⟩ ⊗ |+⟩
Entangled: (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2

sections.title: 4.2 Four Bell states
sections.description: These four orthogonal states are maximally entangled two-qubit pure states. A relative minus sign matters even when one measurement basis hides it. With appropriately chosen settings, Bell-state correlations can violate a Bell inequality and exclude local hidden-variable explanations under the test assumptions. Entanglement does not make every measurement arrangement a Bell test.

sections.title: 4.3 Reading Bell states
sections.description: Computational-basis measurements distinguish the Φ family from the Ψ family, but cannot distinguish the + and − members within either family, even with repeated preparations in this basis. Squaring amplitudes hides the relative sign. If both qubits can be jointly processed, CNOT(q0,q1) followed by H(q0) and computational-basis measurement distinguishes all four ideally.
sections.diagram:
Φ±: P(00)=P(11)=1/2
Ψ±: P(01)=P(10)=1/2
Bell decoding: CNOT(q0,q1) → H(q0) → measure both

workedExample: Use IQLRS order |q1 q0⟩. Starting at |00⟩, H(q0) gives (|00⟩+|01⟩)/√2. CNOT with control q0 and target q1 maps |01⟩ to |11⟩, producing |Φ+⟩. Measuring q0→c0 and q1→c1 gives c1c0=00 or 11 equally likely. For the Bell decoder above, Φ+, Φ−, Ψ+, Ψ− map respectively to 00, 01, 10, 11 (up to global phase).
keyTakeaways:
• Pure entanglement means failure to factor across the two subsystems.
• Relative Bell phases do not change computational-basis probabilities.
• Joint Bell decoding can reveal phase distinctions.
• Bell tests require suitable measurement settings; entanglement does not enable signalling.

questions.question: Which state is specifically |Φ+⟩?
questions.explanation: Φ+ has equal positive amplitudes on 00 and 11. The second choice is the different Bell state Ψ+.

questions.question: Can computational-basis measurements distinguish |Φ+⟩ from |Φ−⟩?
options: No, both give 00 and 11 with probability 1/2 each
questions.explanation: The relative sign disappears in squared magnitudes in this basis; a Bell decoder can distinguish them.

questions.question: Which criterion identifies entanglement for a pure two-qubit state?
options: It has four nonzero basis amplitudes
It cannot be written as a tensor product of two single-qubit states
questions.explanation: Nonfactorization is the pure bipartite criterion. A product superposition can have all four amplitudes nonzero.

learningObjectives: Identify entanglement for pure two-qubit states.
Construct |Φ+⟩ using H and CNOT.
Explain which Bell-state distinctions computational-basis measurements hide.

title: Module 5 – Deutsch‑Jozsa Algorithm
objectives: State the constant-or-balanced promise and its limits. Compare deterministic classical and quantum oracle-query counts. Trace phase kickback and predict the two-input-qubit example.
introduction: Deutsch–Jozsa illustrates how interference can answer a global question about a function. For n≥1, f:{0,1}^n→{0,1} is promised to be constant or balanced. The standard ideal algorithm distinguishes these cases using one quantum oracle query. Its advantage must be interpreted within that promise and query model.

sections.title: 5.1 Promise and classical comparison
sections.description: Constant means every output is the same; balanced means exactly half are 0 and half are 1. Functions outside those cases are outside the promise. An exact deterministic classical algorithm needs 2^(n−1)+1 queries in the worst case: after half the distinct inputs give the same answer, either case remains possible; one more matching output rules out balance. Different outputs establish balance under the promise. Randomized classical sampling can achieve a fixed bounded error with a number of queries independent of n, so this is not an exponential advantage over every classical algorithm.
sections.diagram:
Promise: constant OR balanced
Exact deterministic classical worst case: 2^(n−1)+1
Ideal quantum: 1 oracle query

sections.title: 5.2 Reversible oracle and phase kickback
sections.description: The oracle acts as U_f|x,y⟩=|x,y⊕f(x)⟩, where ⊕ is XOR. Prepare its target in |−⟩ using X then H on |0⟩. Since X|−⟩=−|−⟩, the oracle leaves the target separable and multiplies each input amplitude by (−1)^{f(x)}. One use of this whole oracle counts as one query, even if building it takes many elementary gates.
sections.diagram:
U_f(|x⟩ ⊗ |−⟩) = (−1)^{f(x)}|x⟩ ⊗ |−⟩
Input: |0…0⟩ → H on each → U_f → H on each

sections.title: 5.3 Interference and the decision
sections.description: Measure all n input qubits after the final Hadamards. The amplitude on 0…0 is Σₓ(−1)^{f(x)}/2^n: its magnitude is 1 for constant functions and 0 for balanced ones. Thus all zeros means constant; any other string means balanced under the promise. A single selected input bit is not sufficient in general. Oracle construction, other gates, readout and hardware noise lie outside the one-query count. IQLRS can express simple hand-built oracles; it does not automatically synthesize arbitrary truth tables.
sections.diagram:
Constant: P(0…0)=1
Balanced: P(0…0)=0
Outside promise: no classification guarantee

workedExample: Let the input string be x1x0=|q1 q0⟩, with target q2. The table f(00)=0, f(01)=1, f(10)=0, f(11)=1 is f(x)=x0. Prepare H(q0), H(q1), X(q2), H(q2); use CNOT(q0,q2) as U_f. After the query the input state is (|00⟩−|01⟩+|10⟩−|11⟩)/2 = |+⟩⊗|−⟩. Final H(q0), H(q1) gives |01⟩. Measure only q0→c0 and q1→c1: displayed c1c0 is 01 with probability 1. The target is not part of that readout. For constant f=0, the identity oracle instead yields 00.
keyTakeaways:
• Deutsch–Jozsa is a promise problem, not a classification of every Boolean function.
• One quantum oracle query contrasts with 2^(n−1)+1 exact deterministic classical queries in the worst case.
• Phase kickback and interference suppress or preserve the all-zero amplitude.
• Query complexity does not include oracle synthesis or equal practical runtime; randomized comparisons differ.

questions.question: For n=2, a function has three zero outputs and one one output. What does Deutsch–Jozsa guarantee?
questions.explanation: This function is neither constant nor balanced, so it violates the promise.

questions.question: What does “one quantum query” count?
options: One elementary gate for the whole computation
One use of U_f, excluding preparation, other gates and readout
questions.explanation: The query model counts calls to the supplied oracle. The oracle itself may require many gates.

questions.question: For n=3, how many queries can an exact deterministic classical algorithm require in the worst case?
questions.explanation: Four matching outputs still allow constant or balanced. A fifth matching output forces constant under the promise: 2^(3−1)+1=5.

learningObjectives: State the constant-or-balanced promise and its limits.
Compare deterministic classical and quantum oracle-query counts.
Trace phase kickback and predict the two-input-qubit example.

title: Module 6 – Grover's Search
objectives: Explain a phase oracle followed by diffusion. Compare search query complexity with total implementation cost. Calculate success probabilities to choose a small-instance iteration count.
introduction: Grover search amplifies marked-state amplitudes without reading out every candidate. For one marked item among N candidates, unstructured classical search takes O(N) queries in the worst case, while Grover uses O(√N) oracle queries for high success probability. This quadratic query advantage is not a guarantee of faster wall-clock time for every search problem.

sections.title: 6.1 Phase marking
sections.description: Let f(x)=1 mark a solution and f(x)=0 otherwise. The phase oracle is U_f|x⟩=(−1)^{f(x)}|x⟩. Start in |s⟩, an equal superposition over N=2^n basis states. A phase flip alone changes no computational-basis probabilities; diffusion is needed to turn phase differences into amplitude differences.

sections.title: 6.2 Diffusion
sections.description: One Grover iteration applies the oracle and then D=2|s⟩⟨s|−I. For amplitudes aₓ, diffusion maps each to 2ā−aₓ, where ā is their mean. Intuition: reflect amplitudes about their average after marking. This builds up the marked amplitude for an appropriate number of iterations; applying too many can reduce success.
sections.diagram:
Equal superposition → [phase oracle → diffusion] repeated k times → measure
D: aₓ → 2ā − aₓ

sections.title: 6.3 Choosing iterations
sections.description: For M known marked items with 0<M<N, define θ=arcsin√(M/N). Ideal success after k iterations is sin²((2k+1)θ). Choose an integer near the first peak k=π/(4θ)−1/2, checking nearby integers. For M=1 and large N, the leading estimate is (π/4)√N; it is not an exact count or a certainty guarantee. If M is unknown, choosing iterations requires additional strategy.

workedExample: For N=4 with |11⟩ marked, H(q0), H(q1) prepares amplitudes (1/2,1/2,1/2,1/2) in order 00,01,10,11. CZ(q0,q1) marks 11, giving (1/2,1/2,1/2,−1/2), whose mean is 1/4. Diffusion gives (0,0,0,1), so one ideal iteration succeeds with probability 1. In IQLRS, implement diffusion by H on both, X on both, CZ(q0,q1), X on both, H on both. This gate sequence equals D up to a harmless global minus sign. Finite hardware noise can spoil the ideal certainty; no generic oracle generator is implied.
keyTakeaways:
• The quadratic advantage concerns oracle queries for unstructured search.
• Phase marking alone leaves probabilities unchanged; diffusion converts phase structure into amplification.
• Iteration count depends on N, M and the desired success probability.
• Three iterations beat two and four for the first peak at N=16, M=1.

questions.question: For one marked item and large N, how does the number of Grover iterations to reach the first success peak grow?
questions.explanation: The first amplification peak is reached after a number of iterations proportional to √N; each iteration uses one oracle query.

questions.question: For N=16 and one marked item, which of k=2, 3, 4 gives the highest ideal success probability?
questions.explanation: sin²((2k+1)arcsin(1/4)) gives approximately 0.90845, 0.96132 and 0.58170. The first useful peak is at three iterations.

questions.question: What does the phase oracle alone do to computational-basis measurement probabilities?
questions.explanation: Multiplying an amplitude by −1 preserves its squared magnitude. Diffusion then changes the amplitude distribution.

learningObjectives: Explain a phase oracle followed by diffusion.
Compare search query complexity with total implementation cost.
Calculate success probabilities to choose a small-instance iteration count.

title: Module 7 – Quantum Teleportation
objectives: Trace the three-qubit teleportation protocol. Map measured bits to receiver corrections using IQLRS ordering. Explain why teleportation neither copies an unknown state nor signals faster than light.
introduction: Teleportation transfers an unknown quantum state to a receiver’s qubit using a shared Bell pair and two classical bits. It transfers state information, not matter. The sender does not retain another copy, and classical communication is essential before the receiver can complete the protocol.

sections.title: 7.1 Prepare and measure
sections.description: Put the unknown |ψ⟩=α|0⟩+β|1⟩ on q0. Alice holds q0 and q1; Bob holds q2. Starting q1 and q2 in |0⟩, prepare their Bell pair with H(q1), CNOT(q1,q2). Alice then applies CNOT(q0,q1), H(q0), measures q0→c0 and q1→c1, and sends both bits to Bob. These gates followed by measurement implement Alice’s Bell measurement.
sections.diagram:
Shared pair: H(q1) → CNOT(q1,q2)
Alice: CNOT(q0,q1) → H(q0) → measure q0,q1
Send c0 and c1 to Bob

sections.title: 7.2 Correction convention
sections.description: IQLRS displays a two-bit register as c1c0 (most significant bit first). Before correction Bob’s conditional state is X^{c1}Z^{c0}|ψ⟩ up to global phase. Apply X if c1=1, then Z if c0=1. Label bits before using a table: a source displaying c0c1 swaps the meanings of 01 and 10.
sections.diagram:
Displayed c1c0 → correction on q2
00 → I
01 → Z
10 → X
11 → X then Z

sections.title: 7.3 Why there is no copy or signal
sections.description: After Alice’s measurement, her original qubit no longer holds the unknown input state. The two classical bits select a correction, not a classical description of α and β. Before those bits arrive, Bob’s local state is an equal mixture with no information about the input. This connects to Module 3’s no-signalling principle. Exact recovery assumes ideal operations and a perfect Bell pair; noise changes the fidelity.
sections.diagram:
Unknown state + shared Bell pair + two classical bits
→ corrected receiver state (ideal protocol)
No retained input copy; no faster-than-light communication

workedExample: Take |ψ⟩=(1/√3)|0⟩+√(2/3)|1⟩ on q0 and run the stated protocol. Displayed c1c0=10 means c1=1 and c0=0, so Bob has X|ψ⟩=√(2/3)|0⟩+(1/√3)|1⟩. Applying X alone restores |ψ⟩. The outcome 11 requires X then Z. Each Alice outcome has probability 1/4 independent of |ψ⟩. IQLRS can express these measurements and conditional gates manually; the lesson link does not automatically build this circuit.
keyTakeaways:
• Teleportation uses one shared Bell pair, Alice’s measurement and two classical bits.
• Use c1 for X and c0 for Z with the stated wiring.
• The receiver recovers the input up to global phase in the ideal model.
• Alice retains no copy of the unknown state; classical communication preserves causality.

questions.question: Why must Bob receive Alice’s classical bits?
options: They contain the values of α and β
They identify which Pauli corrections to apply
They create a second copy of the state
questions.explanation: Alice’s bits select a correction; they do not reveal the unknown amplitudes. Without them Bob cannot recover the input locally.

questions.question: With q0→c0, q1→c1 and displayed c1c0=10, which correction does Bob apply?
questions.explanation: c1=1 selects X; c0=0 means no Z. Reversing the displayed bit convention would change the label, not the protocol.

questions.question: Which description correctly explains no-cloning in this protocol?
options: It works only for known classical states
Alice’s measured qubits no longer retain the unknown input while Bob recovers it
The classical bits encode a complete copy of |ψ⟩
questions.explanation: The protocol transfers an unknown state without leaving its original copy at Alice. A universal operation that copies arbitrary unknown states is forbidden by no-cloning.

title: Module 8 – Shor's Algorithm Overview
objectives: Trace the reduction from factoring to order finding. Distinguish the roles of modular exponentiation, QFT and classical post-processing. Verify the N=15 example and state the scope of Shor’s complexity claim.
introduction: Conceptual overview: Shor’s algorithm factors integers in time polynomial in their bit length, roughly log₂N, in the standard quantum computational model. No polynomial-time classical factoring algorithm is known. The advantage over the best known general classical methods is superpolynomial (often loosely called exponential); those classical methods have subexponential complexity in bit length. This is not a proven lower bound against every possible classical algorithm. IQLRS does not provide a full Shor or modular-exponentiation implementation.

sections.title: 8.1 Factoring becomes order finding
sections.description: For an odd composite N (after classical checks for easy cases such as even numbers and prime powers), choose 1<a<N. Compute gcd(a,N): a nontrivial gcd already gives a factor. Otherwise a is coprime to N. Its order r is the smallest positive integer with a^r≡1 (mod N), also the period of a^x mod N. Finding any exponent returning 1 is not necessarily finding the order. Recall: “mod N” means the remainder on division by N.
sections.diagram:
Choose a → gcd(a,N)
If coprime: find least r>0 with a^r mod N = 1

sections.title: 8.2 Quantum information about the period
sections.description: A quantum circuit coherently computes modular powers over a superposition of exponents. Fourier interference produces measurement information related to fractions s/r; measurement does not generally output r itself. In the phase-estimation formulation, an inverse quantum Fourier transform converts phase information into a bitstring. Classical continued fractions, candidate checking and sometimes repeated samples are needed to infer the order. The QFT alone does not perform factoring.
sections.diagram:
Superposition → controlled modular powers → inverse QFT
→ measured y → classical inference from y/2^t ≈ s/r
→ check candidate order (t is the readout register size)

sections.title: 8.3 Turn a useful order into factors
sections.description: If the verified order r is even and a^(r/2) is not −1 modulo N, compute gcd(a^(r/2)−1,N) and gcd(a^(r/2)+1,N). These yield nontrivial factors under these conditions. An odd order, an unhelpful half-power or an inconclusive sample requires another attempt. GCD and continued-fraction calculations are classical parts of the algorithm.
sections.diagram:
Useful even r → b=a^(r/2) mod N
Check b≠N−1
Factors from gcd(b−1,N), gcd(b+1,N)

workedExample: Classical illustration of the reduction, not a Shor circuit: N=15 and a=2 are coprime. Powers modulo 15 are 2,4,8,1 for exponents 1,2,3,4, so the least positive order is r=4. Then a^(r/2)=2²=4; gcd(4−1,15)=gcd(3,15)=3 and gcd(4+1,15)=gcd(5,15)=5. Contrast a=14: r=2 but 14^(r/2)≡−1 mod 15, giving only trivial gcds 1 and 15. The builder link is available for exploring supported gates, not executing full Shor.
keyTakeaways:
• Factoring reduces to order finding with classical checks and possible retries.
• Quantum Fourier interference supplies samples; classical processing infers and verifies an order.
• The polynomial complexity is in input bit length, not the value N.
• The small arithmetic example does not implement the full quantum algorithm.

questions.question: Which sequence best describes the factoring approach?
options: QFT directly returns both prime factors
Order finding supplies r; classical checks and gcds can then yield factors
Measuring the input integer reveals its factors
questions.explanation: The quantum subroutine helps infer an order; classical processing verifies it and uses suitable even orders to obtain factors.

questions.question: Shor’s polynomial-time claim uses which input size?
options: The number of bits representing N
The number of prime factors alone
questions.explanation: Representing N uses about log₂N bits. Polynomial in N would instead be exponential in that bit length.

questions.question: What does the QFT stage provide in order finding?
options: The order r directly on every shot
A proof that every choice of a will factor N
Measurement information for classical inference and verification of an order
questions.explanation: Fourier samples relate to fractions with denominator r. Continued fractions and checking candidates are classical steps; retries can be necessary.
